1:
The pronoun in the first clause is not in the Greek, and the catena supplies five different words for it. Clarke says plainly that with him is not in the text, reports that some supply with you and one ancient version seems to have read so, but notes that no manuscript has it, and himself supplies only the word apostles. Gill agrees the phrase is absent and renders the single Greek word fellow-workers, meaning with one another. Barnes lays out both possibilities, that the apostles were joint labourers with each other or co-operated with God, and reports a scholar who takes the word as a vocative addressing Paul’s fellow-labourers — an opinion in which, he says, that man is probably alone and has departed from the scope of the passage. Ellicott grants the pronoun may be referred to God or to Christ, and decides for the former on the tone of the context. Robertson makes it partnership with God. Calvin allows both, that the particle relates to God or to the endeavours of ministers in common. Wesley takes a fifth course and refers it to the hearers themselves, fellow-labourers with you who are working out your own salvation.

What the working consists in is drawn out by two. Calvin says it is not enough to deliver the message unless one presses it: after the instructions of the embassy are communicated, ministers must add continual exhortations so that their labour be not in vain, since it is the part of an ambassador to enforce by argument what he brings in his prince’s name. Henry honours the office and limits it in the same breath, since ministers are co-workers with God and yet under him, as instruments only; and the language of the gospel is not roughness but mildness and gentleness, beseeching in order to overcome the natural unwillingness of sinners to be reconciled.

On the receiving in vain the notes converge and then divide over who is addressed. Robertson gives the phrase its literal force, into emptiness: the plan of God, the work of Christ on the cross and the pleas of the ambassador may all be nullified by the man who receives the message. Ellicott presses the point on the baptised: those written to had believed and received the grace, but the freedom of the will remained, and by choosing evil they would frustrate the end the grace was meant to work out. Barnes says the offer may be heard and pressed and yet wholly lost, since to hear of the plan of salvation will no more save a sinner than to hear of medicine will save the sick; and these words were addressed to professors of religion, who must guard against self-deception. Wesley states the condition in a line: we receive it by faith, and not in vain if we add persevering holiness. Clarke identifies the grace itself as the great sacrificial offering of Christ.

Chrysostom alone asks why the warning follows so closely on the entreaty. Since the apostle had said that God beseeches and ambassadors are sent, men might grow supine on the strength of it; so he alarms them again, urging that they make haste to please God rather than take their ease. And he sets a term to the beseeching: do not suppose, because he has sent some to exhort you, that this will always be so, for it lasts until the second coming and no longer, and after that is judgment. He presses the shortness of the time as an argument on its own.

Two blocks here are not about this verse. The one under Tertullian expounds the previous chapter, the earthly tabernacle and the house not made with hands, arguing that the dead shall regain their bodies. And the long note under Barnes opens with hundreds of words of numbered remarks continuing the chapter before, reaching this verse only at its end.
2:
Three notes agree that the quotation interrupts the argument. Ellicott says the construction of the third verse is resumed from the first, the second being parenthetical; Robertson calls it another of the apostle’s parentheses. Clarke would read the verse immediately after the close of the preceding chapter, since where it stands it greatly disturbs the connection between the verses on either side, and he prints the passage in the order he prefers.

On the use made of the prophet, Barnes is unusually frank: the words are quoted not as affirming that they are used in the sense for which they were first spoken, but as expressing the idea the writer wished to convey. Clarke prefers to show the fit exactly, noting that the citation follows the Greek version word for word, and giving the Hebrew phrases behind it — the ministry of reconciliation now exercised in full force being itself the proof that the prophecy is fulfilled. Ellicott assumes the apostle had the whole context in mind, and recalls that the words were addressed first to the servant of the Lord as a light to the Gentiles. Calvin makes the fit turn on a relation rather than a text: the Father there appoints his Son a leader for the gathering of a Church, and since Christ was heard in our name we are all admonished in his person not to slight the opportunity offered. Gill takes the person addressed to be Christ and enumerates the hearings, in the garden and on the cross. Wesley reduces it to a proportion: as of old there was a time when God poured out his peculiar blessing, so there is now.

Two notice that the apostle strengthens the word he found in his source. Robertson observes that where the Greek version has the simple verbal he employs a double compound meaning well-received. Ellicott says the same by feel, that the second word for accepted is much stronger than the first, entirely acceptable being perhaps its best equivalent. The editorial matter printed with Calvin makes a third observation of the kind, noting that the version he cites has the simpler word and guessing he was led into the stronger one by its occurrence later in the verse.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse as none of the others do, preaching it to catechumens as the season of confession: confess in an acceptable time and receive the heavenly treasure; blot out all earthly care, for you are running for your soul; and having spent so many circles of the years busied in vain about the world, have you not forty days to be free for your own soul’s sake?

The charge of giving no offence is read as autobiography. Gill takes it as the apostle’s account of himself and his colleagues, who knew men were waiting to vilify the ministry and took care to lay no stumbling-block before Jew or Gentile. Barnes makes the point institutional: not one man would be reproached but the ministry itself, since the misconduct of one preacher brings reproach on the profession and prevents the usefulness of others. Ellicott hears a distinction in the two forms of the Greek negative and takes it as the writer’s own estimate of his aim, avoiding offence not from fear of censure for himself but that the ministry be not blamed. Robertson notes that the noun stands here alone in the New Testament and the Greek doubles its negative. Clarke glosses it as any scandal by which Jew or Gentile might take occasion to vilify the gospel. Calvin sets it in the quarrel: the writer paints in his own person a living picture of a good and faithful apostle, that the Corinthians might see how unfair they were in preferring empty blusterers before him — the very things he cites to his own commendation having probably been urged by them as grounds of contempt.
4:
Robertson alone maps the passage before entering it: the catalogue runs in three aspects, governed in turn by in, by by, and by as, each word carrying a story that could be filled in from the writer’s own life. Ellicott catches the tone instead. The verb is the one already used twice in this epistle for self-commendation, and he hears the writer harping on it: yes, he does commend himself, but by acts and not by words, challenging comparison with men who carried letters instead — and what follows was certain to expose him to the cynical sneer again, of which his generous indignation makes him nobly regardless. Gill and Barnes take it more simply as living so as to commend the office, Barnes adding that a minister who murmured under imprisonment would undo all his preaching, and that God places his ministers in trial partly that they may illustrate their own precepts by example.

Ellicott corrects the word rendered patience to endurance, much stronger than the English; Calvin defines it as the regulation of the mind in adversity, an excellence that ought invariably to distinguish a good minister.

The opening triad is taken apart three ways. Ellicott gives the root-ideas in order — being pressed upon, a constraint that leaves no choice, being so hemmed in that no way is open — while admitting the writer may have used the words without formal classification. Clarke reaches the third sense by a picture, a man driven into a corner as Israel was at the sea, the water before them, the pursuing host behind, fortresses on either hand, so that God alone could bring them out. Wesley makes the three a gradation of hope: in afflictions several ways of escape may appear, though none without difficulty; in necessities one only, and that difficult; in distresses none at all. Robertson translates the last as tight places.

Calvin draws a distinction the others do not. Some things enumerated are required of every servant of Christ; others are not, since a man need not have been tried by stripes and imprisonments to be one, and these will sometimes be wanting in the experience of the best. What is required of all is the disposition to present themselves to be so tried, if the Lord sees fit.

At the particulars the notes turn to biography. Gill counts the beatings, thrice with rods and five times with the scourge of forty save one; Barnes and Ellicott locate each item in the history, the prison at Philippi and tumults at half a dozen named cities. On tumults Clarke prefers insurrections raised against them to the sense of being tossed to and fro; Robertson makes it instabilities, often political; Wesley, attacks a man cannot stand against but which bear him hither and thither by violence. Calvin, who reports a second reading of the word as being frequently forced to change country, is more interested in what the praise consists in: not that the man was unmoved by tumults, since that is common among riotous persons, but that he was thrown into no alarm by tumults stirred up through the fault of others. Two things are required of ministers, that they endeavour to the utmost to maintain peace and yet go forward undaunted through commotions, not turning aside though heaven and earth should be mingled.

The last pair divides them. Ellicott takes both watchings and fastings as voluntary, nights of vigil and self-imposed abstinence rather than privations of the work. Clarke splits the second, partly constrained through want of food and partly voluntary, as a means of obtaining increase of grace for himself and the churches; and he takes the labours to cover both working with his own hands and the spreading of the gospel. Robertson renders the watchings as sleeplessnesses, and adds that the writer knew all about it.
6:
The first word of the second list is narrowed by one and widened by the rest. Ellicott says the cognate adjective elsewhere is decisive for purity from sensual sin, that is chastity, natural to dwell on given the morals of that city. Clarke makes it simplicity of intention with chastity of life; Gill, purity of doctrine and conversation; Barnes, integrity and sanctity generally, a good man being one of the essential requisites even of an orator.

The second word divides them cleanly. Ellicott says the knowledge meant is not of earthly things but of the mysteries of God, and Clarke agrees. Calvin takes it the other way, allowing it may mean doctrine but preferring skill in acting properly; Wesley reads it as prudence, worldly prudence being the practical use of worldly wisdom and divine prudence the due exercise of grace.

The mention of the Spirit among a list of graces raises a question two of them answer. Clarke reports a doubt among learned men whether the third person is meant or some disposition of the soul so denominated, and quotes a rabbinic ladder rising by cleanness, sanctity and humility to the Holy Spirit. Calvin dismisses as frivolous the inference of an earlier expositor that the other excellences must be peculiar to the apostle because the Spirit is named separately — as if they came from any other source. Ellicott sees a reference both to gifts such as tongues and to the promptings in which the writer traced the Spirit’s guidance. Robertson stops at the last item: love without hypocrisy is the only love worth while.

On the power of God, Barnes reports that most older commentators explain it of miracle, but thinks it includes every display of divine power.

The armour is equipment to three and necessity to one. Clarke identifies it with the panoply of the other epistle, assigns the shield to the left arm and the sword to the right, and calls it far-fetched to read the right hand as prosperity and the left as adversity. Robertson divides it the same way, offensive weapons right and defensive left. Wesley says simply, on all sides. Calvin explains why arms are spoken of at all: all who serve God must fight, the devil being always on the alert, and the armour must be complete because if he fails in one onset he attacks from another quarter. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the same words for a description not of a man but of the Church, which by that armour, and by honour and dishonour, crowned the martyrs under persecution and now receives her honours from kings — and while the kings of particular nations have bounds set to their authority, she alone extends without limit over the whole world.

The last pair is where the personal note breaks through. Robertson observes that the preposition has changed from instrument to condition, notes that both words for report stand here alone in the New Testament, and adds that a later book puts the word deceiver in the mouth of the apostle’s adversaries — such slander from enemies being praise. Barnes makes the same point, that the preposition denotes not the means but the medium. Wesley divides them by distance: honour and dishonour when present, evil and good report when absent — and asks who could bear honour were it not balanced by dishonour. Ellicott hears the sensitiveness of a recent experience, a glory not sought and an ignominy not deserved, the word deceiver being most galling of all to a man conscious of his truthfulness. Calvin makes it the severest test of the lot, since nothing is more unpleasant to a noble spirit than disgrace, and few men of heroism have not fallen back when irritated by insults; not to be moved by disgrace is a rare virtue, but one without which no man can show himself a servant of God.
9:
Ellicott reads the whole series as answers to things actually said, and reconstructs the taunts. The word unknown he takes as a jibe at obscure antecedents, answered by the fact that wherever the writer was known at all he was recognised for what he was. Behind dying, and behold we live he hears the exultation of men who had heard of a sentence of death, and supplies their words — his course will soon be over, he will not trouble us long — against which the answer is that he is still in full energy, chastened but not delivered over to death. At sorrowful he asks whether we are still among sneers, and thinks it likeliest that the Jewish rivals or the jesters of the city taunted him with a want of cheerfulness, saying he was always in trouble. At poor he prefers the rendering as a beggar, and supposes the daily work at the tent-cloth and the gifts accepted from another church furnished occasion for a jest.

Robertson reaches the same first pair by grammar: ignored as nonentities without proper credentials, and yet fully recognised by everyone who really matters — a career, he says, full of paradox. Gill locates the ignorance precisely: not their outward estate but their spiritual and eternal state, since the world neither knows what life they live nor what they live upon; and unknown may further mean not owned but slighted and hated. Barnes takes it of men travelling as strangers without introduction from the great, and turns it into a charge against ministers who among strangers lay aside their character. Clarke sharpens the first term into suspicion — men suspected of dark designs, of neither birth nor respectable connections — and answers from the record: they are traceable from place to place, having preached openly and done nothing in a corner. Wesley keeps it theological, that the world knows them not because it knew him not.

On the chastening Clarke presses an argument the others do not: they continue in the very course supposed to have brought these chastisements on them, which, if it were criminal, would justly expose them to death for incorrigible obstinacy; that they are preserved instead is itself proof that they please God.

The sorrow divides into two readings. Barnes takes it as the world’s estimate of religion: seeing only the trials, men suppose Christians must be always sad, since joy is thought to belong to the gaieties of this life and sadness to religion — and he concedes half of it, that they are serious, and their seriousness is often interpreted as gloom. Wesley makes the sorrow real and internal, for our own imperfections and for the sins and sufferings of our brethren, balanced by present peace and a sure hope. Clarke supposes considerate men judging from the outward state that these must be the most miserable of men. Robertson lists the places where the paradox recurs.

The enriching of others produces the sharpest disagreement here. Robertson says the riches meant are spiritual. Clarke argues the opposite materially: the gospel betters the condition of the poor, since it makes them sober so that they save what they before spent riotously, and diligent so that they employ usefully the time they squandered; they both save and gain by religion, and these must lead to an increase of property.

At the close the notes turn admiring. Robertson calls it the climax of the panegyric on the Christian ministry, observes that a narrative thread broken off four chapters earlier is now resumed, and marks the play between the simple verb for having and the compound for holding fast. Wesley ends on the possession, since all things are ours if we are Christ’s, and calls it a magnificence of thought. Clarke limits the all things to what is necessary to preserve life. Gill notes only that the sorrow is outward.
11:
The sudden address by name is noticed as a break. Ellicott hears the dictation stop: the rush of thought has reached its height, the writer rests, and feels almost as though an apology were needed for so vehement an outpouring — and nowhere else in the epistles is there a parallel to this form of speech. Wesley says he seldom uses the appellation and that it has here a peculiar force. Clarke calls the preceding verses a very fine specimen of powerful and commanding eloquence. Henry finds the opposite difficulty: though happy in a great fluency of expression he seemed to want words for the warmth he felt, and opened his mouth so freely because his heart was so enlarged.

The two figures are settled by grammar and by feeling together. Robertson makes the first verb intransitive, a mouth standing open, the sign that nothing has been kept back in the portrait of the ministry; he adds that the second verb occurs in the New Testament only here and in the notice of the broadened phylacteries. Calvin treats the open mouth as a sign of boldness, comparing the promise of an opened mouth to a prophet, and defines the enlarged heart as the cheerfulness that springs from benevolence, noting that Chrysostom takes substantially the same view, since what warms a thing widens it. Barnes puts it as cause and effect: the heart was full, and full hearts make free words. Chrysostom’s own note here is a recapitulation rather than a comment, running back over the catalogue of trials, the paradoxes of sorrow and riches, and the embassy, before letting the address stand as their climax.

The second verse turns the figure round, and one note attacks the English. Barnes explains that the Greek word denotes the upper viscera, applied to the parts of a victim eaten at a sacrifice and thence to the seat of the gentler affections — and objects that our word names the lower viscera and by no means expresses the idea. Clarke takes the other word from a man pent up where there is scarcely room to breathe. Ellicott makes the contrast one of capacity: in that large heart there was room for them and a thousand others, while the narrowness lay in hearts straitened by passions and prejudices which would not make room for him. Robertson suspects that adversaries may have induced some of them to tighten up their affections. Calvin lays it to a corrupt judgment, which is why what he says is not relished; Gill offers the alternative that the readers are not brought into straits by him at all; Wesley says their hearts are shut and so not capable of the blessings they might enjoy.

The request at the end is small and is said so. Barnes states what is not asked — not silver or gold, but only a return of love — and Wesley that nothing hard is asked. Clarke reduces it to four words, love me as I love you. Ellicott prefers to render the noun as a return, and grounds the claim in the relation, since children should requite the care of parents and these are his spiritual children. Robertson finds the noun a rarity, unattested outside this passage, one other verse and later Christian writers, so that it was taken from the vernacular or coined; and no verb is expressed to govern it. Calvin observes that the reproof is softened by the address to them as sons, and explains the recompense as the mutual duty between father and children; the editorial matter printed with him supplies a Greek term for that duty formed from the name of the stork, with an account of the bird’s feeding of its parents in old age. Gill records that three ancient versions render the clause three ways, the last as a demand for repayment of what is owing.
14:
What the yoking forbids divides them sharply. Wesley says the apostle particularly speaks of marriage, though the reasons hold against any needless intimacy. Clarke denies it flatly: the term is military, meaning to leave one’s own rank for another, so the charge is not to desert the Christian community for the heathen — and while he grants the exhortation may be applied to marriages of the pious with the irreligious, that is certainly not its meaning here. Gill denies it too, and denies that civil society is forbidden, since believers must then go out of the world; nor can marriage be meant, such marriages having been allowed lawful in the former epistle. Robertson takes the middle ground, that marriage is included but other unions may be in mind, and notes from the present imperative that the sense is stop becoming so yoked, which implies some were already guilty. Calvin narrows it to idolatry: they frequented the banquets of unbelievers and shared in profane rites, thinking themselves innocent. Ellicott takes both, since the baser party might think it indifferent whether they married a heathen or chose their friends among the worshippers of Aphrodite.

The word is a coinage. Ellicott says it is found nowhere else and was probably made for the occasion, its sense fixed by the law against breeding cattle with a diverse kind and the ban on ploughing with an ox and an ass together — another explanation referring it to the yoke of a balance. Robertson counts the five words that follow, fellowship, communion, concord, portion and agreement, and turns one on his own day, a pertinent challenge where church members wink at violations of the laws of the land and of God. Barnes takes the third musically: there is as much discord between Christ and Belial as between instruments that produce only jarring sounds.

The name Belial produces the most learning in the chapter and no agreement. Gill lists the variant spellings and three derivations, making it without ascent, or a man who never prospers, or a breaker of the yoke of God. Calvin says the Hebrews themselves are not agreed; the editorial matter printed with him adds that the reading Beliar has been restored by several modern editors and that both external and internal evidence favour it. Barnes gives the literal sense as worthlessness and notes that the Syriac simply translates it Satan. Ellicott notes that this is its only occurrence in the New Testament and that it does not appear in the Greek Old Testament at all; that the English version, following the Vulgate, treats it as a proper name; and that this produced the belief, shown in Milton, that it was a fallen angel and the representative of impurity.

At the temple the argument closes. Barnes says it would be as absurd for Christians to mingle with the world as to erect a heathen image in the temple of the Lord, and quotes a scholar that the language can hardly be paralleled in the best classical writers. Clarke puts the incompatibility as absolutes, that an idolater never worships the true God and a Christian never worships an idol, and presses the indwelling: not as a wayfaring man who tarries for a night, but taking up constant residence. Wesley catches what the sentence does not say — not the temple of idols, since idols do not dwell in their worshippers. Ellicott and Robertson both call the promise that follows a composite citation, Robertson adding that its opening clause is found in none of the passages drawn on. Calvin observes that the fault was dealt with at length in the former epistle and contents himself here with a short admonition. Cyril of Jerusalem turns the same questions against a sect of his own century, asking what the majesty of the Church has to do with their abomination: here is order, here is discipline, here is purity.
17:
Both verses are patchworks. Ellicott calls the first a composite quotation and the second a mosaic of citations, assigns each clause its source, and adds that the word rendered Almighty is the usual equivalent in the older version for the Lord of hosts. Robertson observes that it occurs in the New Testament only here and in one other book.

Ellicott then reconstructs how the passage came to hand: the close connection of the verse quoted with the great prophecy of the atoning work makes it probable that in writing of that work the apostle had remembered, or actually turned to, that chapter as it stood in the Greek, and so was led on to the verse standing just before it.

What the words meant first, and how they are used now, is put frankly. Barnes says the summons was addressed to the Jews in exile, that Babylon in Scripture is the emblem of whatever is proud and opposed to God, and states the principle plainly: the language is not used as though it had original reference to Christians, but as containing a principle applicable to the case, the New Testament writers often using the Old so. Ellicott says the historical meaning has passed away for the apostle, the unclean thing being now the whole system of heathenism. Gill reports that the Jewish writers take it as a call to leave the lands of captivity, and that the words are applied elsewhere to mystical Babylon, a call to God’s people to leave her superstitions. Calvin explains the circumlocution by which the prophet describes the priests, who had charge of the vessels, and infers that if so much purity was required of those who carried them, how much more in the vessels themselves — the editorial matter adding a gloss that every believer bears a vessel sacred to the Lord, namely himself.

Clarke makes the whole promise conditional: is it not plain, he asks, that God would be their God only on the ground of their taking him for such, and that this depended on their being separated from the workers of iniquity? Those who would have the promises fulfilled must come under their conditions. He then proposes, as earlier in the chapter, a re-ordering of the text, the first verse of the following chapter belonging to this one. Wesley says only, keep at the utmost distance from him, and reads the receiving as into God’s family.

At the promise of adoption the notes turn warm. Barnes says no relation is more tender and no rank more elevated, and the poorest may reflect that they are children of the ever-living God — how poor are the honours of the world beside it. Wesley makes the promise once given to a king the property of all believers, and asks who can express the worth or conceive the dignity of this divine adoption. Clarke measures it by the difference between fathers: earthly fathers may fail to provide, since everything is not at their disposal and they may lack power or means though willing; but he who made and governs all things can lack neither. Gill guards the sense of the verb, since this is not the beginning of the relation nor its first manifestation, but God’s continuing to act the part of a father, and at last giving the inheritance. Calvin turns the honour into an argument for holiness: what injury we do to God if, while we call him father, we defile ourselves with the abominations of idols. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the adoption as the theme of a charge to those finishing a fast, promising that the Lord will sprinkle clean water on them and that the soul which was formerly a slave has taken her own Master for her kinsman, and drawing from the prophet a twofold grace, of water and of the Spirit, or of the two Testaments.
